headlines.title: Restaurant chains refocus on food quality to bring back diners
headlines.summary: Wendy's, Burger King, Chipotle and other chains are upgrading menu staples as restaurants look beyond discounts to win back diners.
headlines.article_text: Restaurant chains upgrade food to win back diners Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Restaurant chains like Chipotle Mexican Grill and Applebee's are upgrading their core menu items to try to win back diners. For some companies, like Wendy's and Burger King, improved food is a key step in ambitious turnaround plans. In 2009, Domino's Pizza won over customers with an improved pizza recipe and ads that criticized its old version. New Burger King restaurant on the Strand in London, U.K., Oct. 2, 2025. Mike Kemp | In Pictures | Getty Images Juicier chicken tenders. Revamped sauces. Richer and creamier Frosties. Across the restaurant industry, chains are turning their focus back to their food in the hopes that better quality will win back diners. Over the last two years, consumers have dined out less frequently and grown pickier about where they choose to eat, based on data from Black Box Intelligence. In that time, "value" has been the buzzword du jour for restaurant executives, who have explained to analysts and investors that the word encompasses more than menu pricing alone. Now, industry CEOs are turning to their corporate chefs to try to beat rivals on quality and taste, as they look to expand their definition of value. Discounts and one-off promotions can lift traffic for a time, but the actual product still matters for restaurants' long-term growth, as well as franchisee profitability. From Wendy's to Chipotle Mexican Grill , chief executives touted new or upcoming improvements to menu items on their quarterly earnings conference calls in recent weeks. "We think the product's improved and even better," Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright told analysts on the company's call in late October, referring to the burrito chain's brisket, which returned to menus for a limited time Thursday. Turnaround playbook For some chains, better food is a key step in ambitious turnaround plans. For example, "quality food at real value" is one pillar of Wendy's five-part turnaround strategy that the chain unveiled on Thursday. "We're also rebuilding our food offerings and have begun testing improvements to quality and craveability of our core items, including thicker, crispier bacon, a richer and creamier Frosty, whole leaf lettuce on sandwiches and improved salads," Wendy's CEO Bob Wright told analysts on the call Thursday. That same day, the company reported its seventh straight quarter of same-store sales declines and publicly rejected a $1.4 billion takeover bid led by Nelson Peltz's Trian Partners. Wendy's said the proposal did not take into account the potential value that its turnaround plan could unlock. There is precedent to suggest that better-tasting food can contribute to higher sales. In 2009, Domino's Pizza changed its recipe , swapping out its sauce, adding garlic to its crust and switching to shredded mozzarella with a hint of provolone. Along with blunt commercials that compared its previous crust to cardboard and old sauce to ketchup, the changes helped to spur U.S. same-store sales growth of 9.9% the following year. Now, some of the same team that led the Domino's turnaround is copying the playbook at Burger King's U.S. restaurants. Part of the burger chain's multiyear comeback plan has focused on revamping its core menu items. It started earlier this year with its flagship offering, the Whopper, which received a better bun and a new mayonnaise. And in September, it rolled out an overhaul of its nuggets, switching to 100% white meat, crispier breading and a more flavorful marinade. It also reformulated its sauces. "We've tried to look at our biggest categories first," Josh Kobza, CEO of Burger King parent Restaurant Brands International , told CNBC. "We've also thought about the ones where the fixes are more straightforward and less operationally involved." Following the changes, Whopper sales were up by a double-digit percentage in the third quarter, Kobza said on the company's earnings call in late October. And nugget sales climbed more than 35%. Burger King said its U.S. same-store sales jumped 8.4% in the quarter. Like Domino's, Burger King is highlighting diners' past gripes with its Whoppers and nuggets in its ads , which star Burger King U.S. president and former Domino's executive Tom Curtis. Enhancing a strength Better-tasting food isn't just for chains that are in trouble. Even Chili's, which has seen its same-store sales soar 52% over the past three years, is improving more of its existing menu options. After tackling its baby back ribs, burgers and nachos, it will turn next to salads and steaks, Brinker International CEO Kevin Hochman told CNBC. "We're going to be doing more dry aging of our beef to make it more tender, versus doing it in a plant," he said. "It's a little bit more expensive, but we think the taste is going to be a whole lot better." Chili's rival Applebee's launched a juicier chicken tender during its latest quarter, according to John Peyton, CEO of the chain's parent company Dine Brands . In 2027, Applebee's plans to overhaul more of its protein options. "We think proteins are, number one, our biggest opportunity," Peyton told CNBC. "Number two, they're a big focus of the way people are thinking about eating right now, leaning into proteins and a little bit less with the carbs." Chicken is also a focus for McDonald's , which is testing hand-breaded wings, strips and a sandwich in a handful of Chicago-area restaurants. It plans to expand the trial to more locations in the U.S. and Ireland in early 2027. Moreover, McDonald's is trying to improve its coffee, with fresher beans and upgraded equipment, executives said at the company's investor day in September. Both chicken and coffee are fast-growing categories, offering more opportunities to lift sales than McDonald's signature beef burgers. While the burger giant isn't in full turnaround mode like rivals Wendy's and Burger King, its U.S. business has struggled in recent quarters after its value strategy didn't gain the traction the company had hoped. In the third quarter, its U.S. same-store sales fell 0.2%. In addition to menu tests, McDonald's is also leaning into training to improve the quality and consistency of its core menu items. Starting in October, the company launched "Make It Golden," a multiyear training program for corporate employees, restaurant workers and franchisees. Ultimately, improved menu items mean little if the recipe changes aren't well executed. headlines.title: CoreWeave confronts 'doom cycle' narrative as neocloud credit risk overshadows growth
headlines.summary: Leading neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius have both lost about half their value in the past month as they get set for earnings reports this week.
headlines.article_text: CoreWeave confronts 'doom cycle' as credit risk overshadows growth Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Leading neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius have both lost about half their value in the past month as they get set for earnings reports this week. Yields on some CoreWeave bonds are trading above 16%. Last week's midterm elections, which produced sweeping victories for Democrats, added to uncertainty about the pace of the AI buildout. In this article CRWV Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator is interviewed on CNBC's Squawk on the Street at the New York Stock Exchange in New York on Feb. 27, 2026. Michael M. Santiago | Getty Images After a tumultuous month for neoclouds that saw stock prices cut in half, investors are eager to hear how the leading companies in the space plan to navigate a tightening credit market and an unfavorable political environment. CoreWeave is set to report quarterly results on Tuesday, followed by Nebius on Thursday. Both companies are reliant on debt to fund their purchases of cutting-edge artificial intelligence systems, but they're confronting a skeptical base of lenders as the AI trade sours on Wall Street. The neoclouds had a particularly rough day last Thursday, suffering dramatic drops and contributing to the Nasdaq's steepest slump in 19 months. Leading chipmakers Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices and Micron also plummeted on concern that raging anti-AI sentiment would further complicate buildout plans. Nvidia, a major investor in a number of neoclouds, including CoreWeave and Nebius, faces its own fresh turbulence after CEO Jensen Huang admitted Sunday that he'd had an extramarital affair with a business executive who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy. That news could add further volatility to an already nervous market. CoreWeave vs. Nebius over past month Democrats last week won governors' races in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas, and voters rejected data centers in all but one of the 41 related measures on ballots across the country. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator took to LinkedIn to try to temper investors' fears. "We currently don't anticipate any impact to CoreWeave's existing customer commitments or associated backlog as a result of shifts in the political landscape," Intrator wrote. But the market was unrelenting. Yields on some CoreWeave bonds maturing in 2031 jumped above 16%. The spread on its five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, soared above 1,240 basis points, up 50% in the past month. "I do agree completely that neoclouds in particular are going to be the most impacted," Anastasia Amoroso, chief investment strategist at Partners Group, told CNBC's "Closing Bell" on Friday. Unlike hyperscalers Amazon and Microsoft , the top neoclouds are unprofitable and heavily dependent on a small number of customers. IREN , a smaller publicly traded neocloud, said in its earnings report late Thursday that about 48% of its backlog was tied to Microsoft. But the company provided some relief to the market after reporting that AI cloud revenue more than doubled from the prior period. IREN's stock jumped 20% on Friday, recouping its losses from Thursday. Daniel Roberts, co-CEO of IREN, told CNBC that there's a "disconnect between what we're seeing in public market and what we're seeing at the customer level," but he acknowledged the challenge posed by financial markets. "Capital markets have become more selective in the last few weeks, and the questions have undoubtedly moved from how big the contract is to whether it can be delivered, financed, and run at a profit," Roberts said on the earnings call. His company currently has $10 billion in debt. 'How to close this financing gap' At the end of June, CoreWeave was sitting on $5.5 billion in cash and $35 billion in debt. The company owed $1.3 billion at a 15% interest rate on a facility that comes due in March 2028, and had $3.2 billion in obligations on an August 2030 facility at an 11% rate, according to the latest earnings statement . CoreWeave is unlikely to go bankrupt in the near future, and it has the funds to deliver on existing contracts, but growth over the next five years will require more capital, said Luke Yang, a Morningstar analyst covering CoreWeave. "If they want to issue money through equities, the stock price is not working in their favor, because the stock has been beaten down," Yang said. "So I also want to see how management talks about how to close this financing gap." Yang said he's also paying attention to the broader neocloud market. Nscale, based in the U.K., filed paperwork for an IPO in September but hasn't published an updated prospectus since then. "I wouldn't say it's a good time for them to go public," Yang said. SB Energy, which filed at the beginning of September, is in a similar predicament, and Australian neocloud Firmus nixed plans for an IPO last month. watch now VIDEO 4:13 04:13 Freedom Capital's Paul Meeks: CoreWeave shares may triple Power Lunch The uncertainty has not helped CoreWeave's case, Intrator told employees in an October memo seen by CNBC. "But these companies are trying to raise enormous amounts of capital without the execution, revenue, scale or software solutions that CoreWeave delivers to its customers," he wrote. Investors are still on watch. Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets, told CNBC's "Power Lunch" on Thursday that the narrative is "just so negative." "Unfortunately, it's a self-fulfilling prophecy, a doom cycle, where if the creditors are worried about CoreWeave paying back their debts, then of course they have to borrow going forward to fund their AI infrastructure build at exorbitant rates," he said. CoreWeave generated $5 billion in revenue in 2025. Meeks estimates that number jumping to $42 billion in 2028, with an EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization) margin that year of close to 70%. "If they can get on that path and folks feel comfortable with that path, then they'll feel more comfortable about the debts and CoreWeave's financial wherewithal to pay those debts." For the most recent quarter, analysts expect revenue growth of about 160% from a year earlier to $3.55 billion, according to LSEG. Nebius is expected to report sixfold growth to about $908 million. Meeks said he expects the market to get "some relief" from both earnings reports. CoreWeave declined to comment. Nebius didn't respond to a request for comment. For Meeks, the key is getting capital markets back on board with the neoclouds' growth story, and believing that profits are on the way. "You can have a healthy bank, but if there's a run on banks generally speaking then they could be in some trouble," he said. "So I am not fool enough to downplay the credit risk."
